In And Circumcenter C

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: Move a triangle's corners and watch two little lines: one joins two equal-length marks, the other joins two special centres.
How to play: Drag the dots A, B and C, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes for names, circles or the centres, and press Reset to start again.
Look for the math

The question fixes angle C at 30° and asks for two things at once: the little segment DE should be equal to IO and at right angles to it. Drag the corners and the surprising part appears: the right angle never goes away, while the equality comes and goes with angle C.

Where D and E sit

Write a = BC, b = CA and c = AB. The applet starts at B and lays a length c along BC to make D; it starts at A and lays the same length c along AC to make E. Hence BD = AE = AB, CD = a − c and CE = b − c, so

CD/CE = (a − c)/(b − c) = (c − a)/(c − b).

The incenter I is the meeting point of the angle bisectors, and O is the centre of the circumcircle of ABC. The line under the board compares the lengths of DE and IO on every picture.

The right angle does not need 30°

Measure the angle at C and the two lengths for any triangle. The relation is

DE = 2 · IO · sin(C)

and the two lines are always perpendicular. That is why the page stresses that the right angle is independent of the 30° premise: at C = 30°, 2 sin(C) = 1, so DE and IO are equal as well. The logic test checks both statements on more than a thousand triangles, including hundreds with an exact 30° angle.

One line through K, L and M

Let K, L, M be where the external bisectors at A, B, C meet the opposite sides. Menelaus' theorem puts them on one line, and CK = ab/(c − b), CL = ab/(c − a) give CK/CL = CD/CE, so the small triangle CDE is centrally similar to CKL. Therefore DE is parallel to KLM. One correction to the article: it prints the three ratios as b/c, c/a, a/b; with ordinary lengths they are their reciprocals, c/b, a/c, b/a. Their product is still 1, so the conclusion is unchanged. Its signed formulas for CK and CL carry the opposite sign to the measured length; the test uses their absolute values.

A radical axis carries the right angle

The three excenters Ia, Ib, Ic form a triangle whose orthocenter is I. Its circumcenter O′ is the reflection of I in O, so O is its nine-point centre and IO is its Euler line. Four points at a time lie on a cyclic quadrilateral, for instance B, C, Ib, Ic. By power of a point, K has the same power in the circumcircle of ABC, the circumcircle of the excentral triangle and that cyclic circle. So K, L and M lie on the radical axis of the first two circles: it is perpendicular to IO, and DE inherits that right angle through being parallel to KLM.

What the original applet shows

The cut-the-knot article now uses a GeoGebra picture, but a 2007 archive of that same address embeds CODE="InAndCircumcenterC" at 450 × 450 with names hidden. Its five switches and its two-pixel guards are kept here. Unlike the sibling applets — one draws the incircle feet, another proves the result with a point F on the circumcircle — this one adds the excenters and the radical-axis proof. Its own logic test compares the drawing with a second transcription of the Java construction on every well-defined triangle in a seeded spread.

Tick Center line, then drag C until the status reads 30°: DE and IO match in length while staying at right angles. Tick Circle A to see the cyclic quadrilateral behind K.
